extracted.intended_audience: general readers of philosophy and literature; students of Montaigne
extracted.subtask_description: An excerpt from Montaigne's Essays discussing the value and dangers of knowledge, ignorance, memory, skepticism, and simplicity; reflective, argumentative prose rather than an instructional rubric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity as a route to happiness
rubrics_metrics.description: If simplicity conducts us to a state free from evil, she leads us to a very happy one according to our condition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne argues that a simple, less inquisitive life can reduce exposure to evils and anxieties produced by excessive knowledge or curiosity; examples include praise of Lycurgus and reports of 'new world' peoples living honestly without letters. Anti-pattern: valuing learning that produces moral corruption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Well-being defined as absence of illness
rubrics_metrics.description: Our well-being is nothing but the not being ill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay emphasizes that humans feel bad more sharply than they feel good (Segnius homines bona quam mala sentiunt). Thus the greatest good is often merely freedom from pain; pleasures often aim simply at removing pain or restlessness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject absolute insensibility to pain
rubrics_metrics.description: Crantor controverts Epicurus' insensibility if it denies perception of first attacks of evils; complete insensibility would 'annihilate man himself.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne accepts some stoic/Epicurean counsel but objects to a state where one cannot perceive pain at all; feeling pain (and pleasure) is necessary to remain human. Anti-pattern: advocating total numbness or suppression of all sensation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophical distraction by recalling pleasures is ineffective
rubrics_metrics.description: The counsel to divert thoughts from present ills by recalling past pleasures (or to remember past happiness) often fails or worsens suffering ('Che ricordarsi il ben doppia la noia' — thinking of pleasure doubles trouble).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne gives the concrete example of a fevered man whose memory of past wine only aggravates his present condition; he criticizes philosophical recommendations that depend on controllable memory/oblivion as impractical or cowardly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ignorance can function as a remedy for evils
rubrics_metrics.description: Ignorance is but a dull remedy for evils ('Iners malorum remedium ignorantia est').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where reason cannot fortify us, ignorance or dulled judgment can palliate suffering and make life more bearable; Montaigne shows ambivalence—praising the practical benefits of ignorance while noting its costs (loss of refinement, exercise of faculties).

rubrics_metrics.name: Curiosity and pride as moral dangers
rubrics_metrics.description: The thirst of knowledge and the desire to become more wise was the first ruin of man; pride diverts from common path and introduces novelty and error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne (with Christian references) treats excessive intellectual ambition as a root of moral corruption and heresy; advises humility and suspicion of presumptuous inquiry into divine matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humility and confessed ignorance as marks of wisdom
rubrics_metrics.description: Socrates' self-examination and assertion that he 'knew nothing' exemplify that the wisest recognize their ignorance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne praises those who, like Socrates, treat their own knowledge skeptically; the rhetorical and moral value lies in modesty and doubt rather than confident dogmatism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skepticism (Pyrrhonism) produces tranquility (ataraxy)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Pyrrhonians suspend judgment (neither affirming nor denying) and thereby achieve a peaceable, temperate condition of life free from the agitations of opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detailed account of how skeptics accept appearances without assent, avoid commitment, and so escape passions like envy, ambition, superstition. Example: their ritual of arguing both sides and refusing to fix judgment. Benefit: inner calm; trade-off: abstention from dogmatic claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical living under skepticism: act on appearances/probabilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Although skeptics suspend assent, in action they follow appearances, customary practice, laws, pilot's skill, season, and probable circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne stresses that skeptical suspension of judgment need not lead to paralysis: one may live by probabilities and practical signs while withholding intellectual assent. Example: going to sea when vessel, pilot, and season seem right.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of dogmatism to reduce conflict
rubrics_metrics.description: Suspending persuasion is better than entangling oneself in the innumerable errors and wrangling divisions produced by dogmatism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne argues that doubt spares one the conflicts and obligations of defending fixed positions, and allows more freedom of judgment and social ease. Anti-pattern: clinging to sectarian positions simply due to birth or habit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divine incomprehensibility; limits of human categories
rubrics_metrics.description: We attribute human emotions/virtues to God ('Immortalia mortali sermone notantes'), but God, being beyond weakness, cannot properly be described by prudence, justice, temperance, or fortitude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne warns against attempting to map human moral categories onto the divine; theological inquiry should be humble. Example: Aristotle's view that God is exempt from virtue and vice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Faith as gift mediated through the simple/ignorant
rubrics_metrics.description: Our faith is not of our own acquiring; 'it pleased God by the foolishness of preaching to save them that believe.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne notes the biblical idea that divine truth is often conveyed through the 'foolish' or simple, suggesting that ignorance can make one more receptive to faith rather than learned disputation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study often reveals the limits of knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: After long inquiry men often confess that all they have gained is knowledge of their own weakness; 'the greatest part of what we know is the least of what we do not.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne cites elders and sages (Pherecydes to Thales, Plato, Cicero) to show that sustained learning frequently results in humility and recognition of ignorance rather than certitude.

rubrics_metrics.name: Memory is unreliable and not wholly subject to will
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Memini etiam quo nolo; oblivisci non possum quo volo.' We remember what we would not and cannot forget what we would.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne uses this to criticize philosophical counsels that rely on voluntary forgetting or selective memory; practical coping strategies that assume control over memory are suspect.
